question.text:
CASE STUDY (Continued from Question 25):
Question 26: Mrs. Sharma invests her Rs. 5 lakh emergency fund in Scheme C (Overnight Fund) at a NAV of Rs. 1,015 per unit. After 30 days, the NAV increases to Rs. 1,016.25. Which of the following BEST explains why the NAV change is minimal?

answer.text: Overnight Funds invest in securities with 1-day maturity, carrying negligible credit and interest rate risk, resulting in very small but stable daily NAV movements
The fund manager is performing poorly and the fund is generating below-average returns compared to equity benchmarks
The NAV is artificially suppressed by the AMC to maintain stability for conservative investors
Overnight Funds have a regulatory cap on the maximum NAV increase permitted per month

explanation.text: The Logic: Overnight Funds invest in overnight securities having a maturity of one business day. Because the underlying instruments mature the next day, there is no question of the fund taking on interest-rate risk, and the workbook places overnight funds at the low end of the debt risk-return hierarchy. The high-liquidity objective and one-day reset of the portfolio explain why the NAV moves in very small, stable daily increments. The Trap: Option B compares overnight fund returns with equity returns, which is an apples-to-oranges comparison since different scheme categories serve different purposes. Option C suggests the AMC artificially suppresses NAV, but NAV must reflect actual portfolio values. Option D is fabricated -- there is no SEBI cap on monthly NAV movement for any fund category. Note: Source pages 38 and 50 describe the one-day overnight maturity, page 245 confirms there is no question of interest-rate risk in overnight funds, and pages 282-283 place overnight funds at the lowest end of the debt risk-return spectrum.
